sekai.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the vending machine that shouldn't be there, the path just stops — worn smooth by one <kanji>generation</kanji> of hikers after another — and the whole valley unrolls below: rivers, rooftops, a train crawling through it like a toy. You did not climb to see a view. You climbed to see the entire <kanji>world</kanji> laid out under your boots.
sekai.reading_mnemonic: 世 gives せ and 界 gives かい, combining to <reading>せかい</reading>.

keizai.meaning_mnemonic: In the temple's back room, the loom keeps working: thread after thread <kanji>passes through</kanji> the frame while the monk drones on. What is threaded today is not cloth but coins, spooled from house to market to house again. That endless circuit of coin passing through the village is the economy.
keizai.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps as a customer named Kay-Zai counts every coin twice, tracking how money moves through the town — konbini, rent, noodle stand. Her name says it: <reading>Kay-Zai</reading> is how you hear <reading>けいざい</reading>, the economy she watches.

seiji.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats have organized themselves into a council. Every evening they gather on the mossy steps, yowling over who gets the sunniest step, who patrols the gate, who rings the enormous bell at dawn, and only once the vote is cast does the yard finally <kanji>calm down</kanji>. It is petty, procedural, and utterly serious — cats running the shrine until it goes quiet is what <kanji>politics</kanji> looks like.
seiji.reading_mnemonic: 政 gives せい, like Sei, and 治 gives じ, combining to <reading>せいじ</reading>.

iken.meaning_mnemonic: That same eye-on-legs from before does not just wander to <kanji>see</kanji> things — it is opinionated, carrying some stubborn <kanji>idea</kanji> behind its stare. It stops at the school gate, tilts back, and clearly does not approve of the new paint job. It plants itself there until someone stops to hear what it thinks. That stubborn, unsolicited stance is an opinion.
iken.reading_mnemonic: 意 gives い and 見 gives けん, like Ken, combining to <reading>いけん</reading>.

setsumei.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane corners you over the empty offering plate. You stall until dawn's <kanji>bright</kanji> floods both shrine windows at once, sun in one pane, moon still pale in the other, till the courtyard glows so hard the cats squint. In that light your excuse turns readable, laid out plain — an explanation you never meant to give.
setsumei.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer corners him over the price hike, so he SETs a sign by the onigiri shelf that MAY as well be scripture, every reason dated. Regulars read the whole <reading>SET in MAY</reading> notice top to bottom — that rundown is <reading>せつめい</reading>.

shakai.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the shrine, dozens of <kanji>company</kanji> signposts stand staked in rows, each with its own altar showing off to the neighbors. At dusk every cocoon splits at once, workers stepping out to <kanji>meet</kanji> at the table where chopsticks wait crossed for each — a crowd of companies, meeting as one: society.
shakai.reading_mnemonic: 社 gives you しゃ, 会 gives you かい, and company plus meet chains straight through as <reading>しゃかい</reading>.

bunka.meaning_mnemonic: Every hiker who reaches the vending machine atop the mountain trail leaves something behind: a scrap of <kanji>literature</kanji>, a haiku scratched in the paint, a coin balanced on the ledge. None of it was ever official, but each new scratch is a small <kanji>change</kanji> to the pile, and by year three the machine has its own rules new climbers learn just by watching — that unwritten pile of shared habits is culture.
bunka.reading_mnemonic: 文 gives ぶん, like Mon-Bun, and 化 gives か, like Kaa, combining to <reading>ぶんか</reading>.

dentou.meaning_mnemonic: Every spring the same families haul the same boat to the riverbank and launch it from the exact stone their grandparents used, hand to hand they <kanji>transmit</kanji> the same ritual down the generations, though the current shifted downstream decades ago. Nobody remembers why it has to be that stone, only that it always has been — that refusal to move is tradition.
dentou.reading_mnemonic: 伝 already reads でん and 統 already reads とう; stack them and you get <reading>でんとう</reading>, tradition spelled out by its own kanji readings.

boueki.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini turns into a swap meet: register unplugged, a sign taped over it reading TRADE ONLY. A schoolgirl trades her spare umbrella for someone's manga volume; an old man trades a fish for two rice balls. No money changes hands, only goods, back and forth under the fluorescent lights. That shuffling exchange is trade.
boueki.reading_mnemonic: 貿 reads ぼう and 易 reads えき, combining into <reading>ぼうえき</reading>.

yushutsu.meaning_mnemonic: You're back on the mountain trail, staring up at that doubled peak stacked mountain on mountain that means <kanji>exit, leave</kanji>. Today it's not hikers streaming down it — it's crates, lashed onto that wheeled wagon-boat hull built for <kanji>transport</kanji>, cresting the summit one by one and vanishing down the far side, gone for good. That line leaving over the mountain is export.
yushutsu.reading_mnemonic: 輸 gives ゆ and 出 gives しゅつ, joining into <reading>ゆしゅつ</reading> — sounds like "<reading>you shoot</reading>" the goods off the dock and out of the country.

yunyuu.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a raft of crates, lashed to that wheeled wagon-boat hull built for <kanji>transport</kanji>, drifts in from the far shore. Each one bumps the bank, tips forward, and ducks its head low exactly like that figure stepping through a doorway to <kanji>enter</kanji>. One by one they dip and climb onto dry land, none of them made anywhere near here. That dripping parade coming ashore is import.
yunyuu.reading_mnemonic: 輸 gives ゆ and 入 gives にゅう, joining into <reading>ゆにゅう</reading> — sounds like "<reading>you, new</reading>" arrivals crossing onto the bank.

zeikin.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the donation box sits atop the mossy steps, and every coin dropped in goes under that same solid roof you know shelters <kanji>gold, money</kanji>. But this roof never stays yours: once a month an attendant hauls the box away and hands a slice to the town office. Money you owned, skimmed before you see it again: tax.
zeikin.reading_mnemonic: 税 gives ぜい and 金 gives きん, combining to <reading>ぜいきん</reading> — sounds like "<reading>zay keen</reading>" on the tax collector's cut.

kakaku.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, exhausted hikers finally reach the vending machine wedged at the very top. They feed it every coin they have, and instead of a drink it spits out one soggy receipt with a single number scrawled on it, fixed in place the same way each cat owns one branch of <kanji>status</kanji>. That number is all anyone at the summit ever talks about afterward: the price.
kakaku.reading_mnemonic: 価 gives か and 格 gives かく, together forming <reading>かかく</reading> — like a clock's double "<reading>cuckoo</reading>" call ringing out the cost.

shijou.meaning_mnemonic: A vendor drags his rig out of the <kanji>city</kanji> — cloth roof snapping, pot lid clanging on every curious nose — and plants it on the exact patch of <kanji>place</kanji> marked by the old stake, right where the sun lands every morning. Others follow, banners rising all around that one staked spot, until the empty ground is wall-to-wall stalls: a market.
shijou.reading_mnemonic: 市 keeps its market reading し and 場 keeps its place reading じょう, so lined up together they simply read <reading>しじょう</reading>.

koujou.meaning_mnemonic: That same staked patch of <kanji>place</kanji> doesn't stay quiet for long. Someone bolts tin walls up around the marker, raising that same steel beam upright as the first mark of <kanji>craft</kanji> on the lot, and wheels in row after row of clattering machines, and by the time the sun swings back over its old spot next morning, the empty ground has vanished under an assembly line: a factory now stands where the stake used to be.
koujou.reading_mnemonic: 工's こう — think Koichi, the konbini king — plus 場's じょう fuse directly into <reading>こうじょう</reading> for factory.

nouka.meaning_mnemonic: Move that same <kanji>house</kanji> — pigeon still skidding off the slick roof, still crash-landing on the outraged pig below — into the middle of a rice field. Whoever drags themselves out at dawn to feed both animals under that one roof, day after day, is the farmer, and the whole roof-and-pig shambles counts as the farmhouse.
nouka.reading_mnemonic: 農's のう leads straight into 家's か — think Kaa, the fire-breathing crow — fusing into <reading>のうか</reading> for farmhouse.

kenri.meaning_mnemonic: At the toll bridge, a stone-faced inspector squats on a stool with a rubber stamp shaped like a fist. He won't discuss it, won't negotiate — no stamp, no crossing. The moment your ticket lands under that stamp, the whole bridge is yours to walk, nobody blinks at you, and you walk off with a clear <kanji>profit</kanji> besides. That stamp is not a favor. It is your right.
kenri.reading_mnemonic: 権 reads けん and 利 reads り, combining straightforwardly into <reading>けんり</reading>.

gimu.meaning_mnemonic: Every dawn, the shrine cat draws bell duty, not by choice but by rotation — just one more <kanji>task</kanji> on the list. It hauls the mallet up the mossy steps, swats the bell once, and slinks back down before anyone notices it was there. It never looks like it wants to, and it never skips a morning. That's obligation: doing the thing whether you feel like it or not.
gimu.reading_mnemonic: 義 reads ぎ and 務 reads む, combining into <reading>ぎむ</reading>.

shinbun-sha.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>new</kanji> spicy man is hauling his fresh-cut tree in when a reporter shoves past to <kanji>hear</kanji> whispers through the gate first. She sprints to the shrine, stakes the earth sign by the altar — a <kanji>company</kanji>, official this morning — and phones the scoop in. New, overheard, incorporated: a newspaper company.
shinbun-sha.reading_mnemonic: 新 keeps its しん, 聞 keeps its ぶん, and 社 keeps its しゃ, so stacked together they simply read 「<reading>しんぶんしゃ</reading>」。

kigyou.meaning_mnemonic: The sheep's roadside <kanji>business</kanji> under the tree starts small — one sign, one stool — but word gets around, and soon it's franchising: other sheep hired, matching signs hung across town, still chewing paperwork at the same unbothered pace. Same ground it started on, just grown big enough to call itself an enterprise.
kigyou.reading_mnemonic: 企 reads き and 業 reads ぎょう, combining into <reading>きぎょう</reading>.

genin.meaning_mnemonic: A heron picks its way across the riverbank, water that starts far off in a quiet <kanji>meadow</kanji>, and taps exactly one pebble loose from the little dam holding back the current. That single pebble rolls, knocks the next, and the whole bank slides into the water in one long crash. Investigators trace it back to that one dislodged pebble: the cause.
genin.reading_mnemonic: 原（げん）＋因（いん）combine directly into <reading>げんいん</reading>.

kekka.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker feeds every last coin into the one vending machine improbably parked at the summit of the mountain trail. The machine groans, shudders, and grinds for a full minute before it finally clatters out — not a drink, just a single crumpled receipt. That sad little slip of paper is the result.
kekka.reading_mnemonic: 結（けっ）＋果（か）combine straight into <reading>けっか</reading>.

oya.meaning_mnemonic: Long after the final whistle blows at Sei's school field, that same straining figure is still wedged in the tree, refusing to climb down until the very last player has gone home — because a <kanji>parent</kanji> doesn't stop watching just because the game is over.
oya.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a stray cat's anxious owner comes bounding up the mossy steps shouting <reading>Oh, ya</reading> every time she spots her cat near the bell, the same worried shout that gives this word its reading, <reading>おや</reading>.

fuufu.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning on the same crowded platform, a <kanji>husband</kanji> and his <kanji>lady</kanji>, complete strangers to everyone else, bow to the arriving train at the exact same instant, same depth, same beat, without ever once looking at each other to check. Commuters who watch it happen twice stop assuming coincidence and start assuming married couple.
fuufu.reading_mnemonic: 夫（ふう）＋婦（ふ）combine straight into <reading>ふうふ</reading>.

shuukan-custom.meaning_mnemonic: That duckling from <kanji>practice</kanji> still can't land one clean flight, but it hasn't missed a single dawn either. Same rock, same launch, same scattered feathers, same untouched bead of milk on the lilypad — every morning, rain or shine. Repetition that rigid stops being practice; it becomes a habit, a fixed custom now.
shuukan-custom.reading_mnemonic: Every day at Koichi's konbini, the same regular runs the same scam by the shoe rack — the <reading>shoe con</reading> — swiping one sandal as the till beeps. Staff set their watches by him: that unbroken daily <reading>しゅうかん</reading> hasn't varied in months.

kokusai.meaning_mnemonic: The walls that turned land into a whole <kanji>country</kanji> don't stop at one border. Push two enclosures far enough and they meet at the mountain trail's marker, walls flush against walls, one vending machine straddling the seam, selling to hikers from both nations without picking a side. That's international.
kokusai.reading_mnemonic: 国 already reads こく and 際 already reads さい; put them together and you get <reading>こくさい</reading>, international spelled out by its own kanji readings.

seifu.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's cats never asked to run anything, but say who decides which offerings the shrine keeps and everyone points at them — the tabby on the steps, the tom who tolls the bell, the kitten who bats stray coins off the ledge. Nobody elected them, nobody undoes it. That's a <kanji>government</kanji>.
seifu.reading_mnemonic: Sei already carries the せい sound, and 府 gives ふ, so stack them and you get <reading>せいふ</reading>, government spelled out by its own kanji readings.

houritsu.meaning_mnemonic: Everyone in town calls her hoary, sue-happy and ancient — she's taken every neighbor to court twice over, the baker for a crooked loaf, the postman for a bent wheel, herself once by accident. She never loses, because she wrote the rulebook the judge still uses. That rulebook is the <kanji>law</kanji>.
houritsu.reading_mnemonic: 法 already reads ほう and 律 reads りつ; stack them and you get <reading>ほうりつ</reading>, law spelled out by its own kanji readings.

gyogyou.meaning_mnemonic: The sheep's <kanji>business</kanji> never leaves the tree, but it stops being small. Hoof-printed contracts go out to every rowboat on the riverbank, crews hauling nets by the ton on the sheep's word alone. The shade-tree stall becomes an entire fishing industry, sheep still chewing the same paperwork — just for a fleet now.
gyogyou.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a fisherman hauls in a net so overloaded he loses his footing and yelps <reading>ぎょぎょう</reading> — twice, sharp — exactly like a sailor shouting <reading>Yo-yo, oh!</reading> as the fishing industry's whole catch crashes onto the dock.

shigen.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a survivalist stranded with nothing, nicknamed She-Gen — short for she generates. Whatever's needed, she makes from scratch: rope from vines, fire from flint, food from traps. People stop asking what she brought and start asking what resources she'll generate next.
shigen.reading_mnemonic: 資 gives its reading し and 源 gives げん, fusing directly into <reading>しげん</reading> for resources.

kankyou.meaning_mnemonic: Split the sound in half: con, like context, and kyo, like Kyoto, a place. Together that's the context of a place — everything surrounding it, not the place itself. That's environment: not the mountain, but the thin air, the switchbacks, and the vending machine humming at the summit.
kankyou.reading_mnemonic: 環 gives its reading かん and 境 gives きょう, fusing directly into <reading>かんきょう</reading> for environment.

mondaiten.meaning_mnemonic: Every Monday at ten — mon dai ten — the same meeting happens: the agenda lists one <kanji>topic</kanji>, and someone circles one line on the whiteboard in red and says this, exactly this, is the <kanji>problem</kanji> point. Not the whole plan, just this one <kanji>spot</kanji> where everything goes wrong. Monday, ten o'clock, one circled line.
mondaiten.reading_mnemonic: 問（もん）＋題（だい）＋点（てん）read straight through to spell out <reading>もんだいてん</reading>.

dansei.meaning_mnemonic: At the edge of the rice field, the <kanji>man</kanji> who's been dragging the plow all day straightens up, wipes his brow, and struts over to the census officer's little folding table by the paddy. The officer takes one look at those plow-dragging arms, stamps the box for his <kanji>sex</kanji> the way Sei always triple-stamps the nature box at school, and checks it without asking a single question: male.
dansei.reading_mnemonic: 男（だん）plus 性（せい）simply combine to give this word's reading, <reading>だんせい</reading>, exactly as the kanji readings predict.
dansei.description: 男性 is the neutral, formal word for “male” — the term you'd see on official forms, medical charts, or in a news report, not something you'd casually call a friend. Everyday speech leans on plainer words for “man” instead.

josei.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, that same kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> from her kanji story does the wash, one arm sweeping through the current in that graceful pose, the other braced on a rock. A monk from Grandma Kane's shrine passes by, glances at the pose, stamps her card for <kanji>sex</kanji> the way the health-form box always gets triple-stamped, and writes one word in his diary: female.
josei.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker named <reading>Jo</reading> collapses at the summit's lone vending machine, which only takes coins from men. She wheezes, '<reading>Jo, say</reading> please,' until someone tapes a fix over the slot: <reading>じょせい</reading> drink free.
josei.description: 女性 is the neutral, formal word for “female” — used on forms, in medical or professional settings, and in news reporting rather than casual conversation between friends.

seinen.meaning_mnemonic: Right at the foot of the scarecrow — that sun-dried <kanji>year</kanji>-board watching one whole loop of seasons — a tiny sprout pushes up, glowing that impossible <kanji>blue-green</kanji> against the dusk, too fresh to remember a single season the board has watched. Young beside a whole year's watch: that's a youth, a seinen.
seinen.reading_mnemonic: せいねん is just 青 read せい plus 年 read ねん chained straight together, exactly how you already know them, giving you <reading>せいねん</reading>.
seinen.description: 青年 describes a young man roughly in his late teens through twenties. It leans literary or formal — you'll meet it in novels, news reports, and set phrases more than in everyday chat.

shounen.meaning_mnemonic: Perched on the scarecrow's shoulder — that <kanji>year</kanji>-worn board that's stood through one whole loop of seasons — sits the tiny scrap left after someone bit a piece out of small: barely anything, barely <kanji>few</kanji>, up there one single loop of the board's watch. That small, that young: a boy, shounen.
shounen.reading_mnemonic: しょうねん is just 少 read しょう plus 年 read ねん chained straight together, exactly how you already know them, giving you <reading>しょうねん</reading>.
shounen.description: 少年 refers to a boy who is still a child — elementary through junior-high age, not yet a teenager stretching toward adulthood. It's also the word behind “shounen” manga and anime, the genre aimed at that age group.
